The U.S. on Friday moved to exempt some Canadian products from 50% tariffs in a bid to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. sources.news_title: Trump removes Canadian products from 50% tariff list ahead of midterms
sources.text:
Trump removes Canadian products from 50% tariff list ahead of midterms
WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump on Friday removed several Canadian products from a list of goods subject to 50% tariffs, less than two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump signed a proclamation exempting plywood sheets, certain paper products, machinery, refrigeration equipment, and selected packing crates and boxes from the tariffs, according to a White House fact sheet.
The administration will simultaneously add certain valves, carpets, waste products and other goods to the tariff list. The changes will take effect on October 30.
The White House said the adjustments were intended "to better serve the public interest" while continuing to counter what it described as Canada's "discriminatory treatment" of US commerce.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who faces a closely contested reelection race in Maine, announced the exemptions ahead of the White House, highlighting their importance to agricultural producers in her state.
Collins said nine categories of products used by Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed industries would be exempted from the tariffs.
She emphasized that farmers and growers in Maine depend on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other Canadian products that are difficult or expensive to replace with American-made alternatives.
Collins said she had repeatedly urged administration officials to provide tariff relief and pursue a broader trade agreement with Canada.
The announcement comes as Washington and Ottawa continue discussions over trade relations, with Trump recently saying Canada was "working hard" to reach an agreement with the United States.

sources.news_title: Trump Is Cutting Tariffs on Canada, 11 Days Before the Midterms
sources.text:
Trump Is Cutting Tariffs on Canada, 11 Days Before the Midterms
Eleven days before the midterms, Trump quietly reshuffled which Canadian goods face his 50% tariffs, and a trade lawyer says more items were added than removed. The small print may matter far less than a brewing court case that could…
Plywood sheets, packing crates, and blueberry harvesting boxes are coming off President Trump’s Canada tariff list. Cocoa powder, vinyl flooring, shampoos, and carpets are going on.
On Friday, October 23, 2026, Trump signed a Proclamation under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. It changes which Canadian goods face his 50% summer tariffs, and he signed it 11 days before the November 3 midterms.
The iShares MSCI Canada ETF (NYSEARCA:EWC) fell 0.41% and closed at $60.69. That small drop makes sense, because the headline sounds bigger than the document behind it. The fund is up 21.63% over the past year, so investors are considering whether it has already priced in a trade peace that hasn’t arrived.
What the Proclamation Actually Changes
The signed text removes plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes. It adds “certain valves, carpets, waste products” and more. The changes take effect Friday, October 30.
Trade lawyer Robert Glasgow said more items were added than removed. He expects a “relatively small impact in the immediate term.”
The broad tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian products stay in place. They apply even to goods that qualify under USMCA (the North American trade pact). They also stack on top of Section 232 tariffs, which are separate national-security duties, so even the exempted goods get only partial relief.
The White House used broad category names and published no full list. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) announced the relief herself and said nine categories of imports used by Maine growers and seaweed harvesters are now exempt.
Why the Midterm Timing Matters
Collins is in a tight race with Democrat Troy Jackson, who said: “Trump’s trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers.” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) called the move a “desperate, 11th hour attempt” to save Collins’ career.
The pressure reaches well beyond Maine: an AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll taken September 24 to 28 found 65% of Americans blame Trump’s policies more than outside factors for high prices.
Trump took a harder line: “Canada is working very hard to make a deal with us, and I hate to say this, but we have all the cards.” Talks broke down in August, and no signed document shows they have resumed.
What Really Moves a Fund of Canada’s Biggest Companies
EWC holds $7.48 billion in assets. Its largest positions are Royal Bank of Canada (NYSE:RY | RY Price Prediction), Toronto-Dominion Bank (NYSE:TD) and Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP), followed by banks, pipelines, oil producers and gold miners. Plywood and packing crates barely register.
A court case could matter more: on October 20, cheese importer Gellert Global Group sued at the U.S. Court of International Trade over the use of the Depression-era statute. A ruling against Section 338 would do far more for Canadian companies than any exemption list.
Ottawa is also taking on some of the damage. On October 21, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced a joint plan of about C$9 billion for steel, auto and mining companies.
What Could Move EWC After the Midterms
The bullish case for EWC depends on the businesses inside the fund. Canadian banks, energy and gold delivered a 13.06% gain year to date even with the 50% tariffs in force.
Entry price is a risk because EWC trades between a 52-week low of $49.31 and a high of $62.71, and it sits much closer to the top. A failed court challenge could push it lower quickly.
A ruling against Section 338 or a deal after the election would remove tariffs that this Proclamation only reduces. Carney has said, “We could sign it this afternoon if the U.S. were there.”
If EWC closes above $62.71 or the trade court rules against the tariffs, the case for a warming is playing out. If November 3 passes with no new talks scheduled, expect the fund to slide lower.

Trump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, as midterms near
Published 12:05 am Saturday, October 24, 2026
With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from the northern state.
The Republican president’s hefty tariffs on Canada have caused friction with the US neighbor to the north while creating problems for American businesses in Maine and other states that rely on certain Canadian goods.
With the November 3 US midterm elections looming and Republicans fighting to retain control of both houses of Congress, Senator Susan Collins had urged the White House to address tariffs on products affecting companies and farmers in Maine, a state that borders Canada.
Collins, in tight Maine race, praises tariff relief
Trump’s order exempted plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and packing crates and boxes, as well as fresh and dried seaweed, the White House said.
The changes take effect on October 30, four days before the election.
Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50% tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order, including carpets, paints, waste, shampoos, cocoa powder, wooden coffins, ice cream sticks, air-conditioning machines, chest freezers, archery equipment and canoes.
Collins said the relief would aid Maine’s blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.
“These producers are a vital part of our state’s economy and support our rural and coastal communities,” Collins said. “Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”
Democrat Troy Jackson is seeking to oust Collins in a race that polls indicate is very close. The two sparred over tariffs at an October 6 debate.
“Trump’s trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers,” Jackson said on Friday after Trump’s action. “Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire.”
Collins did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Jackson’s remarks.
Trump in August imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian imports, which took effect after talks between the two countries collapsed. Canada retaliated in September with tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion in US goods.
Canada and the United States have been in a standoff over the tariffs since Trump imposed them. Trump asserted on Friday that Canada is working on a deal.
Border-state Republicans seek to strike balance
Republican candidates in northern US border states most affected by the tariffs, including Maine and Michigan, are trying to strike a balance between appealing to Trump’s conservative base and winning over independent voters.
In a statement concerning Trump’s action on Friday, White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton said the president “continues to address Canada’s discriminatory treatment of US commerce” and that the new moves are “further refining the scope” of the previously announced tariffs.
Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister responsible for trade with the US, said Ottawa was assessing Trump’s latest tariff change. “Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests,” LeBlanc said in a statement.
The economies of Michigan and Maine have long been intertwined with that of Canada, covering everything from auto parts to lumber to fruit-picking equipment. Republicans may need to win closely contested Senate races in both states in order to maintain their slim majority in the chamber.
“Trump’s desperate, 11th-hour attempt to save Susan Collins’ political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies,” Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement on Friday. “No one will forget how Trump raised prices on thousands of products American families need by slapping trade taxes on goods from around the world.”
Michigan US Senate candidate Mike Rogers, a Republican who previously called for ending the trade war with Canada, praised Trump for imposing tariffs on Canadian trash. “If you’re going to be putting tariffs on anything from Canada, it ought to be the damn trash they’ve been dumping in our state for decades,” Rogers said.
Trump’s threat in September to block Canadian jet maker Bombardier from the US market became a political issue in Kansas, where the company employs 1,500 workers in Wichita. Trump dropped the threatened ban this week after calls from Kansas lawmakers including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is also locked in a tough reelection race.

sources.news_title: Trump Eases Canadian Tariffs In Likely Last-Ditch Attempt To Help Republicans In Tight Midterm Races

Trump Eases Canadian Tariffs In Likely Last-Ditch Attempt To Help Republicans In Tight Midterm Races
The White House announced on Friday that it would slash tariffs on certain Canadian goods following criticism of the government's trade dispute with Canada by Republican candidates in key states.
The administration of President Donald Trump announced on Friday that tariffs on certain Canadian products linked to agriculture would be lifted. The move is expected to help Republican candidates before the midterms, especially long-serving Republican Senator for Maine Susan Collins.
In order to "continue effectively offsetting the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest, President Trump is ... removing certain products — such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes — from the scope of the Section 338 tariffs," the White House said on Friday.
These items will no longer be subject to the tariffs of 50 percent that were initially imposed on a range of Canadian goods in July. These tariffs were, according to the Trump administration, a "response to Canada's discriminatory treatment of American products."
However, the government also announced that there would be a new range of Canadian goods subject to the 50 percent levy, such as "certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others."
The news was welcomed by Republican candidates who are facing tight races against Democrat challengers in key states in the November midterm elections.
Susan Collins, who is facing a tough electoral challenge from her Democrat opponent Troy Jackson as she seeks to win a sixth term as a Maine senator, responded particularly favorably to the news, posting on X on Friday that she was "pleased to have secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers."
"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she added.
Collins noted that she had repeatedly asked for, and would continue to lobby for, tariff relief.
The tariff war between Canada and the U.S. has become a key political issue in other races too; in Michigan, both Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Republican opponent Mike Rogers have criticized the Canadian tariffs and the financial pressure they exert on Michiganders.
Following the administration's change of tariff policy, Rogers reiterated on Friday that he had "called for an end to the tariff war," but praised the Trump administration for placing new tariffs on Canadian "trash trucks," claiming that Canadian trucks have been using Michigan's landfills to dispose of garbage for "decades."
According to a White House proclamation, "residual products of the chemical or allied industries," which are likely the products Rogers is referring to, will now face the 50 percent fine.
A Fox News poll released on Thursday showed Collins and Jackson tied at 49 percent apiece in the Maine Senate race, whereas El-Sayed is leading Rogers by approximately three percentage points in the Michigan race as of October 24, according to MSNOW's Michigan poll tracker.

Trump Ends 50% Tariffs on Some Canadian Goods, Boosting Susan Collins
sources.text:
President Trump on Friday removed 50% tariffs from several Canadian goods heavily used by Maine’s agricultural sector, prompting praise from Republican Sen. Susan Collins as she fights to hold her seat in the New England state.
The exemptions cover corrugated boxes, crates, plastic bags, packing equipment, refrigeration machinery and seaweed, according to a White House proclamation. At the same time, the administration added a 50% duty to several other Canadian imports, including shampoo, vinyl flooring, coffins, carpets and window air conditioners.
Collins said the changes would offer relief to Maine farmers. She specifically cited wild blueberry growers who depend on “specialized harvesting boxes from Canada,” along with apple and potato producers who use Canadian supplies during harvest season.
Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in a state that leans Democratic, said she had pressed senior Trump administration officials to provide “tariff relief for these important products.”
“These producers are a vital part of our state’s economy and support our rural and coastal communities,” Collins said. “Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”
Democrats, however, have denounced the exemptions as a politically driven move.
“After attacking Canada and crushing the American people, I can’t think of a more desperate admission of failed trade policy than temporarily lowering tariffs on select products to favor a political ally 11 days before an election,” Rep. Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, said. “This stunt only proves further that Trump’s trade strategy is not grounded in anything legitimate, but rather in naked politicization and manufactured chaos.”
The goods had been among billions of dollars’ worth of Canadian imports that Mr. Trump subjected to 50% tariffs in late August, after negotiators from the two countries failed to reach a trade agreement. Canada responded by imposing steep duties on certain U.S. products.

Collins has voiced opposition to the trade war while also highlighting her efforts to secure exemptions for Maine, a state that shares a border with Canada and maintains deep economic ties to its neighbor.

sources.news_title: Susan Collins touts Canada tariff relief in tight Maine Senate race
sources.text:
Republican Senator Susan Collins announced Friday that U.S. tariffs will exempt nine categories of Canadian imports used by Maine agricultural businesses after she pressed the Trump administration for relief.
The breakthrough gives Collins a potentially valuable closing argument in one of the country's tightest Senate races, where Democrat Troy Jackson has used Trump's trade war with Canada to attack the Republican incumbent, and polling shows the candidates separated by little or nothing.
The exemptions cover packaging, refrigeration and processing equipment, as well as certain seaweed goods used by Maine blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers, potentially reducing costs for businesses that Collins says have limited alternatives to Canadian suppliers.
Collins said she pursued the exemptions through repeated discussions with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and other Trump administration officials. In announcing the move, Collins said many Maine agricultural producers depend on Canadian equipment, packaging and other supplies that are unavailable domestically or expensive to replace.
The timing gives Collins another opportunity to distance herself from an element of President Donald Trump’s economic agenda that has presented political problems in Maine. Collins has repeatedly opposed broad Canadian tariffs and previously urged the administration to reach a trade resolution with Canada, arguing that tariffs would hurt Maine families, municipalities, manufacturers and farmers.
Newsweek reached out to Jackson’s campaign for comment and was referred to a statement he posted on X.
“Trump’s trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers,” Jackson said, before accusing Collins of enabling the administration’s policies.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House and Collins campaign for comment.
What Canada Tariff Exemptions Did Susan Collins Announce?
The nine categories identified by Collins include:
- Corrugated paper or paperboard boxes
- Plastic boxes, crates and similar products
- Plastic packing bags and sacks
- Refrigeration and freezing equipment
- Machinery used to clean, sort or grade agricultural products
- Filling, sealing, closing and labeling machinery
- Packing and wrapping machinery
- Certain non-adhesive sheets, films, foils and strips
- Seaweed and algae products for human consumption
James Melcher, a professor of political science at the University of Maine at Farmington, noted that the exemptions should not be understood as broadly eliminating tariffs on Maine agricultural products themselves. Instead, much of the relief applies to packaging, machinery and other products agricultural businesses use in their operations.
“It’s NOT removing tariffs on agricultural products themselves; it’s on their packaging,” Melcher told Newsweek.
CNBC separately reported Friday that Collins had announced exemptions covering nine categories important to Maine agriculture.
According to the Republican senator's office, Maine wild-blueberry growers import specialized harvesting boxes from Canada that work with existing processing equipment, while an American producer of some cardboard agricultural totes has stopped making them. Potato and apple growers also use the affected products during harvesting and while preparing crops for market.
Collins' office said removing the tariff on Canadian seaweed would additionally benefit Maine companies in the growing seaweed industry.
“These producers are a vital part of our state’s economy and support our rural and coastal communities,” Collins said in a statement announcing the exemptions. She added that businesses rely on Canadian products “that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”
She also said she would continue seeking further exemptions while pushing for a wider trade agreement with Canada.
Why Canada Tariff Relief Could Matter for Susan Collins
The exemptions arrive at a potentially critical moment for Collins, whose race against Jackson is among the country's closest Senate contests.
The RealClearPolitics polling average through October 20 showed Jackson at 48.8 percent and Collins at 47.4 percent, while a Fox News poll conducted October 16-20 found the candidates tied at 49 percent.
That narrow margin magnifies the political significance of an issue Collins has spent months trying to separate herself from Trump on: tariffs against Canada. Jackson has sought to turn the trade dispute into an argument against the Republican incumbent, including attacking an earlier round of relief during an October debate.
After the administration exempted Canadian road salt and cement, Jackson quipped that Maine residents “can’t eat road salt.”
Friday's announcement gives Collins a broader response to that attack. The new exemptions cover products tied to Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed industries and include packaging, refrigeration and agricultural machinery producers use in their operations.
Collins can therefore point not only to her opposition to Trump's tariffs, but to specific exemptions she says resulted from her conversations with senior administration officials.
For Collins, the timing is significant regardless of the administration's motivation. She is asking voters to return her to Washington while simultaneously arguing that she can use her position to push back against policies from a Republican president when they hurt Maine.
Earlier exemptions for road salt and cement allowed her to make that case once. The agricultural exemptions broaden the group of Maine businesses for which she can now claim tangible relief.
Melcher said the exemptions allow Collins to reinforce a central argument for her reelection: that her long experience and relationships in Washington give her influence she can use on Maine's behalf.
“Like the road salt exemptions she worked on previously, this helps Collins reinforce her theme that she has valuable DC connections she can leverage to help Maine,” Melcher told Newsweek.
Trump’s Canada Tariffs Become a Campaign Issue
The larger trade fight intensified in August, when the Trump administration imposed 50 percent tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods after negotiations between Washington and Ottawa broke down.
Canada responded with retaliatory measures, and the administration subsequently changed the U.S. tariff list by removing some products while applying the duties elsewhere.
Jackson has used that dispute against Collins. During an October debate, the candidates clashed over tariffs, along with abortion and the Iran war.
For Collins, the latest exemptions provide a concrete result she can point to after months of publicly urging the administration to modify its approach. But they do not end the underlying U.S.-Canada dispute, and Collins has previously emphasized that broader tariffs continue to pose risks for Maine businesses and consumers.
The political significance is not necessarily confined to Maine. Published reports noted that Republican candidates in other states with substantial Canadian trade ties have also criticized the administration’s policy, including former Representative Mike Rogers in Michigan and former Senator John Sununu in New Hampshire.
Collins, Maine’s senior senator and a longtime Republican who has frequently positioned herself apart from her party on selected issues, is now seeking another term, with the outcome potentially carrying consequences beyond the state.
For the immediate campaign, however, Friday’s announcement gives her a new argument: her opposition to the tariffs has produced specific exemptions for Maine industries, just as voters decide whether to send her back to Washington.
Biggest Issues Facing Maine Voters
Economic pressure dominates recent polling of Maine voters. A Fox News survey found that only 12 percent said their family was financially better off than two years earlier. More than six in 10 also disapproved of Trump's performance as president.
A University of Massachusetts Lowell-YouGov poll conducted from August 28 to September 14 found that 63 percent of likely Maine voters said paying for basic necessities had become somewhat or much harder during the previous six months.
Asked what was most responsible for higher fuel and utility prices, 61 percent cited the Iran war and another 17 percent cited tariffs, meaning 78 percent attributed the increases to one of those administration policies.
The concerns give the Canada trade dispute additional significance in the Senate race. Collins is presenting the agricultural exemptions as evidence that she can push her party's administration for changes that benefit Maine, while Jackson has attacked the senator over her relationship with Trump and the effects of the administration's policies.

Crucial products for Maine's agricultural industries will be exempt from tariffs, Sen. Susan Collins says
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, announced Friday that nine categories of products, which she said are crucial for Maine's agricultural industries, will be exempted from U.S. tariffs on Canada amid the ongoing trade war between the neighboring countries.
The categories of products receiving tariff exemptions include plastic boxes and crates; plastic packing bags; refrigeration and freezing equipment; packing and wrapping machinery; paperboard cartons and boxes; seaweed and algae products for human consumption; non-adhesive plates, sheets, film, foil and strip; agricultural machinery for cleaning, sorting and grading; and machinery for filling, sealing, closing and labeling.
Collins said the exemptions will benefit Maine businesses and farms that produce blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed.
“These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities. Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," Collins said in a statement.
The latest round of exemptions followed continued conversations between Collins and Trump administration officials, including U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
“In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families," Collins said.
Last month, Collins worked to get the Trump administration to exempt road salt, cement and pulp from the list of tariffed items from Canada.
Collins is running for her sixth term in the U.S. Senate and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has been critical of the senator throughout his campaign, claiming Collins is not doing enough as chair of appropriations to stop tariffs.
“I would just think that someone that is the most powerful senator in the United States Senate would be able to do more than get us road salt back,” Jackson said last month.
On Friday, Jackson said Collins begs for relief from chaos she helped create.
"Trump’s trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire," Jackson said in a statement to Maine's Total Coverage. "Mainers needed help long before Susan Collins needed saving. But apparently, families struggling to pay their bills wasn’t enough of an emergency. Her losing her job is."
Collins said she will continue working directly with the Trump administration to seek additional relief from tariffs.

sources.news_title: Scrambling Trump eyes surprise reversal to rescue Susan Collins: report
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is expected to lift some tariffs on Canadian goods to help Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) and other Republicans in the midterms, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday in an exclusive.
The changes could come as soon as Friday and would likely eliminate 50% tariffs on certain agricultural and forestry products, people familiar with the plans told the newspaper. They cautioned that the timing and scope could change.
Collins welcomed the move in a statement after the report, listing nine types of goods that would be spared, among them some farm machinery, refrigeration equipment and packaging.
“I have asked for tariff relief for these important products and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families,” Collins said. “I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.”
But there could also be a catch. The administration may raise tariffs on other Canadian products to offset the relief, as it did last month when it lifted tariffs on road salt and cement, the Journal reported.
Collins took credit for that earlier exemption on the campaign trail, but her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, shot back during a debate that Mainers “can’t eat road salt.”
Collins, who has broken with Trump on tariffs, is locked in a tight reelection battle against Jackson, whose campaign has hammered her over Trump’s trade war with Canada.
The move could also help Republicans in other trade-heavy states, including former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan and former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire, both of whom have criticized Trump’s Canada tariffs, the Journal reported.
The 50% tariffs, which hit roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods, took effect in late August when last-ditch trade negotiations collapsed.
A White House official called preliminary reporting speculation and said tariff announcements would come from the administration.

The changes will take effect Oct. 30. The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.''

sources.news_title: Donald Trump to lift some Canadian tariffs
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to lift tariffs on some Canadian imports at the end of the month.
The Wall Street Journal reported Friday afternoon that the change is to help Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection bid. Collins’ office and the White House separately confirmed the changes to the tariffs shortly after.
The change is aimed at benefiting the blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed industries, according to a statement from Collins’ office.
It played into the dueling themes of Collins’ toss-up race with Democrat Troy Jackson. She has built her campaign around her ability to negotiate with those around the Republican president while highlighting her disagreements with him on tariffs and other major issues. Jackson has sought to tie her to the unpopular Trump in a Democratic-leaning state.
Collins’ statement said she had stressed the burdens of high costs on Maine businesses and families to key members of the Trump administration.
“I will continue working directly with [federal] officials to seek additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner,” she said.
The tariff exemptions would apply to packaging materials such as cardboard boxes, plastic crates, bags and film; refrigeration and the machinery used to clean, sort, fill, seal, label and wrap farm and food products; and edible seaweed and algae.
Trump imposed tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods in August after trade talks collapsed. Canada answered with its own tariffs last month, though it backed down on a planned 25% levy on Maine lobster before they took effect.
Collins has voted several times to end Trump’s tariffs on Canada while lobbying for item-by-item relief. The administration exempted Canadian road salt and cement in September after she pressed U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
“This is not China we are dealing with,” Collins said in August. “It is Canada, our best friend.”
At a debate last week, Collins cited those exemptions and one for pulp as proof her clout delivers for Maine. Jackson said he would not give her credit for pulling a few items off the tariff list “when we should have never had a list.”
Maine Democratic Party spokesperson Misha Linnehan said Trump knows Collins’ campaign “is in trouble because of her unyielding support for his disastrous agenda.”
“Now, he’s playing politics with our trade policy when Maine businesses and families are already reeling from the chaos of his trade wars,” Linnehan said.
The race is one of a handful that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. The most recent public poll, by Fox News, found the candidates tied at 49% with less than two weeks until Election Day.
Jackson, who was joined by U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at a rally in Portland on Thursday, has held a slight edge in other recent polls. But Collins trailed in every single one in 2020 before handily beating Democrat Sara Gideon.

sources.news_title: Maine senator says she secured tariff exemptions for some Canadian goods
sources.text:
OTTAWA — U.S. President Donald Trump plans to lift 50 per cent import taxes on a host of Canadian goods and impose them on a longer list of new products — changes that prompted a Republican senator in Maine to take credit for duty relief in a key battleground state ahead of American midterm elections.
Presenting the changes as a refinement of the tariffs that Trump slapped on Canada this summer, the White House said the changes would “ensure these measures continue to effectively offset the burden or disadvantage to U.S. commerce from Canada’s discriminatory measures” — an echo of the president’s long-standing claims that Ottawa’s own trade policies unfairly harm U.S. businesses.
Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs are now set to be lifted from 22 classes of Canadian goods as of Oct. 30, according to the White House. These include seaweeds, corrugated paper, plastic boxes, plastic packing bags, refrigeration equipment, and cleaning and grading equipment. Tariffs will also be removed from labelling machinery, packing machinery, non-adhesive plates and other paper and wood products.
New tariffs on Canadian goods
At the same time, Trump plans to impose 50 per cent tariffs on a range of roughly 100 new Canadian products, from cocoa powder to paints and varnishes, soap and shampoo, several types of flooring, carpets, canoes, boat parts, freezers, archery equipment, wood coffins and more.
The White House fact sheet also underscores that Canada and China are the only two countries that “have chosen to retaliate” against Trump’s tariffs “rather than negotiate a deal with the United States.”
It was not immediately clear if the value of the newly tariffed goods was larger than those receiving the relief.
In a statement to the Star, Eve Loignon-Giroux, a spokesperson for Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, said the federal government “takes note” of Friday’s tariff changes and is now assessing their impact.
“Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests,” she said.
Tariff relief ahead of U.S. midterms
But U.S. Sen. Susan Collins was quick to take credit for the change she said would benefit her state of Maine, where she is vying to keep her seat from a Democratic challenger in a race that could help decide which party controls the U.S. Congress after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. In statements Friday, Collins — a moderate Republican in the state that borders Quebec and New Brunswick — said she has “secured” tariff exemptions for nine Canadian products that are crucial for Maine agricultural producers.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in a post on social media Friday.
If the suit succeeds, it could tie Trump’s hands on trade policy tighter than ever, trade lawyer says.
Collins added that she had “repeated conversations” about tariffs with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick about getting tariffs lifted, and that she will keep pushing for more relief.
“I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally, and largest trading partner,” she said.
Canada still waiting for trade deal
Speaking to reporters earlier in Istanbul, Prime Minister Mark Carney gave no indication he expected U.S. tariff relief, and even signalled that a broader trade deal might have to wait until Trump leaves office in 2029.
“We don’t care about the timing of that,” said Carney, stating Canada is ready to sit down with the U.S. if the Americans want to talk in good faith.
“We could sign it this afternoon if the U.S. were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that,” he said.
Arguing the U.S. has been a victim of unfair trade practices, Trump started imposing tariffs on Canada shortly after he returned to office last year. But the trade war intensified over the summer, when the Trump administration hit a broad range of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, beyond the so-called “national security” tariffs that have impacted Canada’s steel, autos, and aluminum sectors.
The new wave of import taxes prompted Ottawa to respond with tariffs of up to 50 per cent on billions of dollars worth of U.S. imports, while Trump followed with a ban on Canadian alcohol and dairy products.

The president has also threatened to increase auto tariffs from 25 per cent to 50 per cent on Jan. 1.
The situation has sparked objections from U.S. politicians in some areas, with declarations that the tariffs are making life more expensive and harming local industries. Collins has pushed back against tariffs as she vies to keep her seat.
Responding to the announcement of tariff relief Friday, the Maine Democratic Party said in a statement that the move shows Trump knows the Collins campaign “is in trouble.”
The Democrats accused Collins of “unyielding support for (Trump’s) disastrous agenda that has made life harder and more expensive for Mainers,” and said Trump is “playing politics with our trade policy when Maine businesses and families are already reeling from the chaos of his trade wars.”
U.S. accuses Canada of interference
The tensions over trade have also seen American officials accuse Canadians of meddling in U.S. politics through efforts – including Premier Doug Ford’s anti-tariff commercials that aired in the U.S. – to sway the American public and officials against Trump’s trade agenda.
In Türkiye Friday, Carney rejected those claims and said he is “disappointed” in U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra for advancing them.
Asked whether those concerns were laying the groundwork to blame Canada if Trump’s Republicans lose out in the midterms, Carney said he didn’t expect that to happen, but noted the U.S. has used a “very broad range of justification” for tariffs on Canada so far.
“It’s up to the United States,” Carney added, when asked if a trade deal could happen before the Nov. 3 vote in the U.S.
“They’re a little hard to predict.”

sources.news_title: CP U.S. to drop some tariffs on Canadian exports, says Maine senator
sources.text:
President Donald Trump speaks to reporters after arriving on Air Force One, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, at Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers, Fla. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
By The Canadian Press
Trump administration dropping and adding some tariffs on Canadian exports
U.S. President Donald Trump is lifting some tariffs on Canadian exports at the end of this month, but adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.
As the trade war with Canada becomes a ballot box issue in key races ahead of November’s midterm election, Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, said Friday nine categories of Canadian exports will be exempted from tariffs. Those include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and several types of machinery important to her state’s agricultural industries.
Collins is in a tough re-election battle and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has made the trade war with Canada a key issue in the tight race.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in a media statement Friday.
Collins said the tariff exemptions are for products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.
The executive order signed Friday by Trump says the tariffs will disappear from those products on Oct. 30, and that the changes are being made after Trump received new advice from senior executive branch officials.
“In my judgment, the modification in this proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States, is required by the public interests, and will better serve the public interest,” the order reads.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to Collins’ announcement of limited tariff relief by posting on social media, “Now get rid of the rest.”
However, the same executive order will also impose new tariffs on dozens of new categories as cocoa powder, paints and varnishes, shampoos, vinyl flooring, archery equipment and carpets. It also will apply 50 per cent tariffs on sewage sludge, and some municipal waste.
Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a political flashpoint in states such as Maine and Michigan ahead of November’s midterms.
Trump slammed an array of Canadian products with 50 per cent tariffs in August after trade talks with Ottawa broke down. The president also signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on specific American imports.
Trump again escalated trade tensions the following month by banning imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some liquor and whey products.
Earlier this week, a U.S. food importer filed a legal challenge against the Depression-era trade statute — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — that Trump used to hit Canada with the heavy duties and trade embargoes.
Collins has repeatedly broken with Trump over his tariffs on Canada. Maine shares a border with Quebec and New Brunswick and relies heavily on trade with Canada.
Collins has argued on the campaign trail that her behind-the-scenes advocacy has secured tariff relief, pointing to the Trump administration’s decision to lift duties on road salt and concrete.
Jackson has countered that Mainers “can’t eat road salt” and small carve-outs won’t reverse the wider economic damage caused by Trump’s tariffs and trade war.
Jackson responded to his challenger’s tariff announcement Friday by saying Collins “enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire.”
“Mainers needed help long before Susan Collins needed saving. But apparently, families struggling to pay their bills wasn’t enough of an emergency. Her losing her job is,” Jackson posted on social media.
“We deserve a senator who stands up to Trump — not one who rubber-stamps his agenda and begs for relief from the chaos she helped create.”
Collins said she has had multiple conversations with United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and other Trump administration officials to ask for tariff relief.
“I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner,” she said.
While Collins has taken credit for the latest tariff relief, it could become a road map for other Republicans in border states trying to navigate Trump’s unpopular policies in their tight races.
The Michigan and Maine races in particular could prove critical to control of Congress. Democrats need to achieve a net gain of four seats to get the Senate majority.
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers also recently broke with Trump over the trade war with Canada, despite previously supporting the president’s policies. He faces a tight race with Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
In a campaign ad posted on social media earlier this month, Rogers said people in Michigan “know that Canada is not our enemy.”
“We need to end this tariff war now,” Rogers said in the ad, which shows the Republican sitting at a bar and holding a Labatt’s beer.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

sources.news_title: U.S. to drop 50% tariffs on nine Canadian product categories, Maine senator says
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump is dropping 50-per-cent tariffs on a handful of Canadian products used by farmers just 10 days before midterm elections, where Democrats could wrest control of Congress from his Republicans.
Maine Senator Susan Collins, a Republican in the midst of a tough re-election battle, said in a statement on Friday that she had successfully lobbied U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to lift the levies on nine product categories.
These include Canadian paperboard cartons, plastic crates, plastic bags, refrigeration equipment, agricultural sorting machinery, non-adhesive foil, and seaweed.
The White House confirmed it would take these products off the tariff list, but said it would replace them with new levies on valves, carpets and waste products to keep the total amount of Canadian-made goods subject to border taxes the same.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in a statement that Mr. Trump was “protecting American farmers, manufacturers, and workers” with his levies.
No timeline to resume formal trade talks with U.S., chief negotiator says
Ms. Collins said in her statement that the agricultural goods are used by Maine blueberry, apple and potato producers, and can’t be easily found elsewhere, while the seaweed is turned into food products by Maine companies.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” she said.
Farmers across the U.S. tend to be a reliably Republican group, but are getting disproportionately hammered by Mr. Trump’s protectionist trade policies and his war on Iran, which have raised prices of farming equipment and diesel.
In addition to Maine, the Republicans are trying to hold on to Senate seats in major farm states such as Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska. Tariffs are a central election issue in other tight races, too, such as Michigan, where the Republicans are trying to take a Senate seat from the Democrats.
Consumer frustration with the cost of living has been the Democrats’ top issue in the elections. In an apparent acknowledgment of how unpopular inflationary policies such as tariffs are, Mr. Trump on Friday insisted to reporters that Canada is “working very hard to make a deal with us” and “we have all the cards.”
But Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking before the President made his comments, said Canada is willing to hold out for a good deal rather than rush the process. Whether a deal happens or not is up to Washington, Mr. Carney told reporters in Istanbul, where he is on a state visit. “They’re a little hard to predict,” he said.
The Prime Minister said he’s willing to sit down and resume talks if the U.S. is willing to bargain in good faith. Ottawa doesn’t care about “the timing” of a deal, he said, even if it takes months “or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place.”
Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded on X to the news that Mr. Trump would drop some tariffs on Canada: “Now get rid of the rest.”
Dominic LeBlanc, the minister in charge of the U.S. trade file, said in a statement that the tariff changes had been noted. “While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith toward a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests.”
Ms. Collins previously took credit for the Trump administration lifting tariffs on Canadian road salt and cement. In that case, too, the White House imposed equivalent tariffs on other Canadian goods. The senator also said she convinced the Canadian government to drop retaliatory tariffs on seafood.
Whether the relatively narrow tariff relief will be enough to help Ms. Collins remains an open question. On Friday, her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, wrote on social media that Ms. Collins “enabled” the tariffs by voting to confirm Mr. Trump’s protectionist officials “and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire.”
Ms. Collins isn’t the only Republican to run away from Mr. Trump’s trade policies.
In Michigan’s Senate race, Republican nominee Mike Rogers has released an ad in which he drinks Labatt Blue, declares “Canada is not our enemy” and calls to “end this tariff war – now.” The trade war has also come under fire from Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who assails the tariffs on Canada in every stump speech.
Mr. Trump has imposed several rounds of tariffs on Canada since returning to power last year and threatening to make the country the U.S.’s “51st state.” Some of the levies are sectoral, including 50-per-cent tariffs on steel and aluminum, and 25 per cent on autos. Others, including the tariffs lifted on Friday, were imposed using the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act and cover $28-billion worth of Canadian goods.
The Smoot-Hawley tariffs, implemented under a law signed by U.S. president Herbert Hoover in 1930, are subject to a court challenge by a New Jersey food importer launched this week.
Canada has retaliated against the U.S. tariffs with levies of its own and tried to negotiate an end to the trade war. Talks collapsed in August and there have been no negotiations since.
Earlier this week, Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator, said the lines of communication are open between the two governments, but there was no concrete plan for getting back to bargaining.
“We’re having conversations to see whether or not we can come back to the table for a set of detailed negotiations. We don’t know exactly when that’s going to happen,” she told a conference in Toronto.

As the Journal elaborates, "Trump in late August applied 50 percent tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods — about 5 percent of its exports to the U.S. — after last-minute negotiations between the nations broke down. Canada retaliated with tariffs of its own, leading Trump to ban the import of certain Canadian products and threaten to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles in January if the sides cannot come to an agreement. The upcoming move would be the second time the Trump administration has altered its 50 percent tariffs on Canada. Last month, it removed tariffs from products including road salt and cement — a decision that Collins took credit for on the campaign trail. The move didn’t deter attacks from Jackson, however, who said during a debate with Collins this month that Maine residents 'can’t eat road salt.'"
While the request came from Collins, the Journal notes that the move could also be an attempt to help other embattled GOP candidates. In Michigan, nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers has released ads calling for Trump to end his trade war with Canada after months of backing the president’s actions. In New Hampshire, former Sen. John Sununu has been similarly critical. According to the Journal, "Trump’s 50 percent tariffs were imposed under a never-before-used trade authority — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, better known as Smoot-Hawley. This week, a New Jersey-based food importer filed a legal challenge against those tariffs, arguing the Trump administration is overstepping its legal authority."

U.S. President Donald Trump is lifting some tariffs on Canadian exports at the end of this month, but adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.
As the trade war with Canada becomes a ballot box issue in key races ahead of November’s midterm election, Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, said Friday nine categories of Canadian exports will be exempted from tariffs. Those include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and several types of machinery important to her state’s agricultural industries.
Collins is in a tough re-election battle and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has made the trade war with Canada a key issue in the tight race.
“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in a media statement Friday.
Collins said the tariff exemptions are for products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.
The executive order signed Friday by Trump says the tariffs will disappear from those products on Oct. 30, and that the changes are being made after Trump received new advice from senior executive branch officials.
“In my judgment, the modification in this proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States, is required by the public interests, and will better serve the public interest,” the order reads.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to Collins’ announcement of limited tariff relief by posting on social media, “Now get rid of the rest.”
However, the same executive order will also impose new tariffs on dozens of new categories as cocoa powder, paints and varnishes, shampoos, vinyl flooring, archery equipment and carpets. It also will apply 50 per cent tariffs on sewage sludge, and some municipal waste.
Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a political flashpoint in states such as Maine and Michigan ahead of November’s midterms.
Trump slammed an array of Canadian products with 50 per cent tariffs in August after trade talks with Ottawa broke down. The president also signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.
Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on specific American imports.
Trump again escalated trade tensions the following month by banning imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some liquor and whey products.
Earlier this week, a U.S. food importer filed a legal challenge against the Depression-era trade statute — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — that Trump used to hit Canada with the heavy duties and trade embargoes.
Collins has repeatedly broken with Trump over his tariffs on Canada. Maine shares a border with Quebec and New Brunswick and relies heavily on trade with Canada.
Collins has argued on the campaign trail that her behind-the-scenes advocacy has secured tariff relief, pointing to the Trump administration’s decision to lift duties on road salt and concrete.
Jackson has countered that Mainers “can’t eat road salt” and small carve-outs won’t reverse the wider economic damage caused by Trump’s tariffs and trade war.
Jackson responded to his challenger’s tariff announcement Friday by saying Collins “enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire.”
“Mainers needed help long before Susan Collins needed saving. But apparently, families struggling to pay their bills wasn’t enough of an emergency. Her losing her job is,” Jackson posted on social media.
“We deserve a senator who stands up to Trump — not one who rubber-stamps his agenda and begs for relief from the chaos she helped create.”
Collins said she has had multiple conversations with United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and other Trump administration officials to ask for tariff relief.
“I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner,” she said.
While Collins has taken credit for the latest tariff relief, it could become a road map for other Republicans in border states trying to navigate Trump’s unpopular policies in their tight races.
The Michigan and Maine races in particular could prove critical to control of Congress. Democrats need to achieve a net gain of four seats to get the Senate majority.
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers also recently broke with Trump over the trade war with Canada, despite previously supporting the president’s policies. He faces a tight race with Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
In a campaign ad posted on social media earlier this month, Rogers said people in Michigan “know that Canada is not our enemy.”
“We need to end this tariff war now,” Rogers said in the ad, which shows the Republican sitting at a bar and holding a Labatt’s beer.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

sources.news_title: US Llifts Tariffs on Canadian Goods Ahead of Elections
sources.text:
The White House announced a partial rollback of tariffs on Canadian goods, effective 30 October. The move comes just weeks before the US midterm elections, raising concerns about how trade policy may affect voter sentiment in key border states. Source: bbc.co.uk.
What Changed
Starting 30 October, tariffs will drop on plywood sheets, some paper products, machinery, and refrigeration equipment. These goods support manufacturing and agriculture in both countries.
At the same time, new tariffs will apply to carpets and waste products. This selective approach shows the policy is not broad but focused on specific sectors.
Who Pushed for the Change?
Senator Susan Collins of Maine first raised the request. She said the exemptions help her state’s agriculture industry, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers.
Collins has repeatedly asked senior Trump administration officials for relief. She plans to continue working with officials to seek more relief and push for a broader trade deal with Canada.
How the Trade Standoff Began
President Trump said the US faced unequal treatment of exports like cars, dairy, and alcohol. He framed the tariffs as a response to unfair trade practices.
Canada matched the tariffs dollar for dollar to protect its workers and industries. It called such actions necessary for domestic competitiveness.
Canadian Response
Canada’s internal trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said the country is assessing the latest US moves. He said Canada remains open to constructive talks and a mutually beneficial trade deal.
Since April 2026, Canada has held nine meetings with the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee. These talks focus on the impact of US tariffs and long-term economic effects.
Political Reactions
Senator Collins’ Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, criticized her role. He said Trump’s trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers.
He claimed Collins enabled the chaos by voting to confirm officials who supported the policy. He said she now seeks credit for actions that only brought a cup of water to put out the fire.
Michigan Republican Mike Rogers also urged Trump to end the trade standoff. His state depends on cross-border trade. He supported the policy in recent ads, showing how trade issues affect political messaging.
Trump’s Position
President Donald Trump said Canada is ‘working very hard’ on a trade deal with the US. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is open to a deal but will wait for a fair resolution.
Carney said: ‘We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that.’
Why This Matters
With midterm elections approaching, trade policy is becoming a political issue. Border states like Maine and Michigan are directly affected.
Any tariff shift could influence voter sentiment and economic stability in these regions.
What to Watch Next
How the trade policy evolves will be closely watched. New negotiations or public statements could shape the political landscape ahead of the elections.
Observers will track whether Canada and the US move toward a broader trade agreement or remain in a standoff.

The administration of US President Donald Trump will roll back a number of tariffs on Canadian goods that have disproportionately harmed residents of US states bordering Canada.
This was announced on Friday by Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine, The Washington Post reports.
The US president is expected to lift the 50% tariffs on products used in agriculture, including corrugated paper boxes and crates; plastic boxes, crates and cases; refrigeration and freezing equipment; purification equipment; and certain types of machinery.
The duties Donald Trump imposed on imports from Canada hit residents of Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire particularly hard. The economic impact has spilled over into three highly competitive Senate races in those states. Susan Collins’s seat is seen as particularly at risk as she seeks re-election in a state where Donald Trump lost the 2024 presidential election.
Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, has made Trump’s trade war with Canada a central campaign issue, and polling in the final week before election day shows them on roughly equal support.
As a reminder, in late August Trump imposed 50% duties on Canadian goods worth about $20 billion—around 5% of Canada’s exports to the United States—after last-minute talks between the two countries collapsed.
Canada responded with its own tariffs, prompting Trump to ban imports of certain Canadian goods and to threaten to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles in January if the sides cannot reach an agreement.
